newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's rebel Laurent Kabila:leader or figurehead?.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's rebel Laurent Kabila:leader or figurehead?.

text.p: Laurent Kabila, political leader or perhaps figurehead of Tutsi rebels in Zaire, is a former Marxist who has fought President Mobutu Sese Seko's rule for more than 30 years.

Kabila, 56, says he is the head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), whose cutting edge is the force of Banyamulenge ethnic Tutsis now controlling much of the east.

"The aim of the alliance is to put an end to Mobutu's autocratic rule and to banish his corruption from Zaire," Kabila told Reuters in an interview last week in Uvira, the first major centre captured from Zaire's ramshackle army.
But the political groups inside the coalition are obscure and analysts say one of Kabila's main assets is that he is not an ethnic Tutsi.
"The Banyamulenge wanted him for his experience and because he is not a Tutsi," said Gerard Prunier, a French academic who specialises in this region of Africa.
Kabila is from mineral-rich Shaba in southern Zaire.
"Kabila is more of a name, just to pretend this is a Zairean rebellion," Belgian journalist Colette Braeckmann, an expert on Zaire, told the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).

War in the east began when the Banyamulenge, a community of 300,000 or so, resisted Zairean attempts to expel them to Rwanda. But its roots go deeper and the rebels have a solid spine of veterans who fought with Rwanda's Tutsis after 1990.
Short and stocky with white-flecked hair, Kabila now looks the part of a mature civilian politician.
He has come a long way since he joined the "Mulele" rebellion in eastern Zaire in the 1960s when the former Belgian Congo narrowly avoided break-up just after independence.

Mobutu, president since 1965 but now sick with cancer in Europe, crushed that rebellion with foreign help. Ironically the Banyamulenge tribe, Tutsi herdsmen who moved to Zaire up to 200 years ago from Rwanda, then fought alongside the Mobutists.
"For Kabila, yesterday's enemies are today's friends," one African diplomat in Nairobi commented.
Kabila's walk in the wilderness began, but he did not waste his time during the 30 years before he made headlines last month.
"He set up shop in the mountains south of Uvira, founding a kind of independent mini-republic," Prunier told Reuters from his home in Paris.
"He and his supporters killed elephants, quite ecologically, and did mining. Then they smuggled the ivory and diamonds and gold through Burundi," he said.
"Kabila is part of the left-wing, anti-Mobutu movement that sprang up in Zaire in the sixties," Prunier said.
Kabila, who speaks perfect English despite coming from francophone Zaire, was a regular visitor to Uganda in the late 1980s after Yoweri Museveni's rebels took power in Kampala.

At exactly the same time, the exiled Rwandan Tutsis holding top positions in the Ugandan army were fine-tuning their plans to invade their homeland. They did so in 1990 and won the civil war four years later after the extremist Hutus in power had exterminated up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

The link, from Museveni to Rwandan Tutsi strongman Paul Kagame to the Banyamulenge rebels in Zaire, is at the heart of claims by Kinshasa and some other African states that a plot is unfolding to create a "Tutsiland" in central Africa.
Kabila says there are four parties in the alliance and the protocol which created it was signed on October 18 this year, in Lemera, the first eastern Zairean town to fall to the rebels.

The parties in the alliance are Kabila's Popular Revolutionary Party (PRP), the National Council of Resistance for Democracy (NCRD) led by Kissante Ngandu, the Revolutionary Movement for the Liberation of Zaire (RMLZ) led by Mosasa Minitaga and the People's Democratic Alliance (PDA) led by Robert Bugera.
None of these men is a household name.
The Alliance says it is committed to a free-market economic system and a pluralist political set-up.
